title: How Bitcoin Works
summary: Josh and Chuck explain Bitcoin: its origins as a digital, decentralized, peer-to-peer currency published under the pseudonym Satoshi Nakamoto in 2008, how coins are created through "mining" and blocks of transactions released roughly every ten minutes, the halving of rewards every four years, the 21 million coin cap, wallets and exchanges like Mt. Gox, security risks such as hacks and the need for backups, price volatility and speculation, and the Silk Road darknet marketplace and related crime and government action. The episode opens with a discussion of the history of US currency (fiat money replacing the gold standard, post-Civil War private bank notes) and closes with a listener mail story about electroconvulsive therapy and memory loss.

segments.title: Opening banter and episode setup
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the tech edition topic, note listener requests for Bitcoin, and joke about accents before turning to money.

segments.title: History of money: gold standard to fiat currency
segments.summary: Hosts describe modern government-issued money, the Federal Reserve's creation in the early 20th century, the thousands of private banks issuing currency during and after the Civil War, and the move from the gold standard to fiat currency.

segments.title: What Bitcoin is and its origin
segments.summary: Bitcoin is introduced as the first entirely digital, decentralized currency with no central authority. Its origin is mysterious; a pseudonym, Satoshi Nakamoto, published a document in 2008 and reportedly mined the first fifty coins in 2009.

segments.title: Double-spending problem and the public ledger
segments.summary: Satoshi's document addressed the problem of copying digital currency and spending it repeatedly, using a public ledger instead of a trusted keeper, with coin creation tied to maintaining the ledger.

segments.title: Using bitcoins: wallets, exchanges and fees
segments.summary: Explanation of how to get bitcoins: set up a software wallet, buy from exchanges such as Mt. Gox, and spend at merchants or convert to cash. Hosts say fees are lower than with bank transfers, and that bitcoin is seen as a digital form of cash because of anonymity.

segments.title: Speculation and the Winklevoss twins
segments.summary: Bitcoin can be held and traded like a stock for speculation; the Winklevoss twins are mentioned as bitcoin holders worth millions.

segments.title: Peer-to-peer network and bitcoin mining
segments.summary: Bitcoin runs on a peer-to-peer network. Miners solve a math problem for each ten-minute block of transactions and the first to solve it receives newly minted coins. The reward halves every four years, with a 21 million coin cap, and the process also keeps the ledger updated and secure. Mining has become costly in electricity and hardware, and individuals rarely mine alone.

segments.title: Security, open source code and hacking risks
segments.summary: The code is open source and the ledger is verified across the network, but exchanges and wallet companies are vulnerable to hacks. Hosts advise keeping backups of wallets on removable drives, citing a user who lost bitcoins when a laptop crashed.

segments.title: Price volatility, Silk Road and government action
segments.summary: Bitcoin's price swung widely from cents to around two hundred dollars, driven by speculation. The darknet marketplace Silk Road sold drugs and other goods; it was reportedly shut down by a blackmailer's DDoS threat. The Department of Homeland Security froze Mt. Gox accounts, and a DDoS attack on Mt. Gox was mentioned.

segments.title: Future outlook and mainstream adoption
segments.summary: Hosts discuss predictions that Bitcoin may not last, that rivals could replace it, and that Amazon has introduced its own coins for the Kindle network. A hitman case involving a metal singer's bitcoin purchase is mentioned.

segments.title: Sign-off and where to learn more
segments.summary: Hosts suggest further reading on HowStuffWorks, Wired, The Economist and Mother Jones, and sign off with a sponsor-style closing.

segments.title: Listener mail on electroconvulsive therapy memory loss
segments.summary: A listener named Chris Pinkerton describes a friend who lost memories of their shared high school years after electroconvulsive therapy for depression, and the hosts respond supportively.
